Apsis holds no model credential and calls no vendor API: model access is a host-declared endpoint, the payload is the command text plus static vocabulary, and no LLM SDK may enter package.json (D27)

no interpreted clause is applied without a span present verbatim in the user's input — filters and the action alike — and unrecognised language is computed by subtracting accepted spans, never read from the model's own report (D28)
with no interpreter declared, resolveCommand returns the grammar's result synchronously: no promise, no timer, no request (CONTRACT_LLM_COMMAND_PARSING §E)

identity is derived from Apsis's own sealed session cookie and NEVER from a request header, query parameter or body: userId, organizationId, roles and capabilities sent by the browser are ignored (D36)
authorization is one question at every endpoint — can(identity, capability) — so roles enter in capabilitiesFor() and no endpoint learns what a role is (D36)
on a protected endpoint the IP limiter runs BEFORE authentication and authentication runs BEFORE the request body is read, so an unauthenticated request is refused before its payload arrives (D37)

a development auth bypass must be ABSENT from the production artifact, not disabled by a flag: it lives outside server/, is imported only by scripts/, and an import-graph test asserts it is unreachable from api/ (D38)

Apsis writes no session cryptography: sealing, JWT validation and refresh rotation are the provider SDK's. @workos-inc/node is server-side only and may be imported by server/auth/provider.ts and its tests alone — not by server/interpret.ts, api/**, or src/** — enforced by an import scan (D39)
D27 is unchanged by the auth SDK: model integration stays fetch-only with no LLM SDK, and no auth SDK, key or token exists in the browser (D39)
a retryable provider refresh failure must never sign a user out: the cookie is kept and the request answers 503 with Retry-After; only a terminal failure clears it and yields 401 (D40)
a rotated sealedSession returned by refresh() must always be written back as the cookie; Apsis must not add a refresh mutex, because WorkOS rotation has a replay grace period (D40)

the interpreter endpoint is not a trusted component: forced tool use narrows model output, but the browser validator governs what reaches LeadQuery and the server trims for size and shape only — never re-deciding truth (D29)
the client's posted `schema` is ignored; the server builds its prompt from its own pinned COMMAND_SCHEMA import, and unknown top-level keys are rejected rather than absorbed (D30)
command text, prompts, model output and envelopes are never logged; logs carry codes, latencies, token counts and error classes (D31)
rate limiting is cost control, not access control: the per-IP bucket is per-instance on serverless, and the endpoint stays unauthenticated until the auth milestone lands (D31)

the provider sends no sampling parameters on any model: Sonnet 5 returns 400 for non-default temperature/top_p/top_k, and a per-model capability table would fail as a production 400 rather than a red test (D32)

the design requires forced tool use, which Fable 5.1/Mythos 5.1 and manual extended thinking reject with a 400 — APSIS_MODEL is free text, so this is documented in the README next to the variable (D32)
every function in api/ must carry supportsCancellation in vercel.json: on Vercel cancellation is opt-in per path, and without it request.signal never fires and abandoned work is billed (D33)

Apsis is a browser-only SPA with no server, so any API key reachable by it is public: it must never hold a vendor credential or call a vendor API directly. Model access goes through a host-declared endpoint, and only the user's command text plus a static schema ever leaves the browser — never leads, names, phones, emails, health information or history (CONTRACT_LLM_COMMAND_PARSING §L)

an LLM may never be trusted to report what it failed to understand: every mapped filter must cite a span present verbatim in the input, and unrecognised text is computed by subtracting verified spans — the same way parseCommand earns it (CONTRACT_LLM_COMMAND_PARSING §H)

current_milestone.name: authentication and access control for /api/interpret
current_milestone.status: contract written and binding, NOT implemented. The endpoint is implemented and deliberately not safe to expose publicly until identity exists at the boundary
current_milestone.approach: managed provider (WorkOS AuthKit) with a hosted sign-in page, server-to-server code exchange, and the provider's SEALED SESSION carried in a cookie Apsis owns. Uses @workos-inc/node ^10.13.0 SERVER-SIDE ONLY (zero runtime and zero peer dependencies) — Apsis writes no session cryptography (D39). No browser SDK, no password handling, NO APSIS DATABASE. Chosen on what happens when agencies arrive: every self-hosted path means building org membership, invitations and roles by hand — and a database — at the moment the product is trying to sell. The provider token already carries sub/sid/org_id/role/permissions
current_milestone.shape: SDK APIs verified against published type definitions, not prose: getAuthorizationUrlWithPKCE, authenticateWithCode({session:{sealSession,cookiePassword}}), loadSealedSession, authenticate(), refresh(), getLogoutUrl() — note the docs render it getLogOutUrl while the types say getLogoutUrl. A retryable refresh failure (rate_limit_exceeded/timeout/server_error/network_error) KEEPS the session and answers 503; only terminal failures yield 401 (D40). Identity is derived from the sealed cookie and never from a header or body (D36); the order is method->origin->content-type->IP limit->authenticate->authorize->per-user limit->body cap->parse->provider, so authentication precedes reading the body (D37); the dev identity lives outside server/, is imported only by scripts/, and is absent from the production bundle rather than disabled by a flag (D38)
current_milestone.v1_scope: gates the INTERPRETER, not the application — the default build still needs no credential and still makes zero requests. TRIGGER for changing that: the moment any real customer data is served from the server, the app-wide gate becomes mandatory
current_milestone.previous_milestone: host interpreter endpoint — IMPLEMENTED and deployment-hardened (D29-D34). POST /api/interpret, same origin, Node 22, plain Request->Response in server/ with a 3-line adapter in api/; Anthropic via fetch with forced tool use; no SDK and no new dependency so D27 stands; default model claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 via APSIS_MODEL. Deployment review closed three defects: temperature:0 would have made APSIS_MODEL=claude-sonnet-5 a hard 400 (no sampling parameters are sent now, on any model, D32); Vercel request cancellation is opt-in per path and is now enabled in vercel.json, without which abandoned requests keep running and are billed (D33); and the rate limiter cleanup ran after the push so it could never fire, leaking an identity table (D34). NO REAL-KEY CALL HAS BEEN MADE — every test uses a fake provider, so the wire format is asserted against the current published API but not confirmed against the live one. The README carries the exact smoke-test command
current_milestone.honest_gap: still unauthenticated until this milestone ships. Two limitations are designed in and recorded rather than hidden: a stolen session cookie stays usable until the provider-configured access-token lifetime lapses, because authenticate() validates locally and WorkOS is only consulted at refresh(); and rate limits remain per-instance cost control rather than durable quotas. Those two are the ONLY things that would justify adding a database, and neither is needed for v1

performance.round5: owner is on SAFARI; dev == production subjectively, retiring the build-mode hypothesis. Enumerated the full graphics/compositor stack and found FOUR backdrop-filter:blur() elements layered directly over the live WebGL canvas (.command-row and .command-out at 14px, .uv-clusters and .uv-skills at 6px)
performance.round6: backdrop-filter CONFIRMED as a real but PARTIAL contributor (owner A/B: noticeable improvement, significant lag remains). Safari ~= Chrome subjectively on careful re-comparison, retiring the WebKit-specific hypothesis. Chrome measured numerically worse while feeling the same, and ALL spans scaled together (~3x), so revisionWalk is explicitly not concluded to be the cause. Shipped ?matrix=1: ten cases, one axis each, identical 8s scripted drag, plus per-frame bad-frame correlation (GPU fence vs spans vs long tasks) to classify GPU-bound vs main-thread stalls
round6_harness_bugs_caught: correlation records stored ms=0 because frame duration was computed after `last` was reassigned — every bad-frame bucket was silently empty while the distribution table looked correct. Fixed and re-validated.
?dpr=1 was unverifiable locally (machine is already DPR 1); checked at simulated Retina, drawing buffer 1600x552 -> 800x276 as intended
performance.superseded_hypothesis: CSS backdrop-filter compositing over the WebGL canvas — work that happens AFTER requestAnimationFrame returns and is invisible to every instrument here. First hypothesis consistent with ALL evidence: JS cheap, frame intervals perfect, fx=off partial, field=off/core=off making no difference (a backdrop blur costs the same regardless of what is behind it), dev==prod, Safari-specific severity. UNTESTED — ?backdrop=off decides it in ~1 minute
performance.not_observable_from_js: true presentation time (pixels on glass) in Safari: no frame-timing API, no long-animation-frame, no EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2. GL execution, WebKit compositing, backdrop-filter evaluation and the vsync handoff are all invisible. Best proxies added: polled WebGL2 fenceSync, rAF lateness, input->handler latency

?backdrop=off and ?overlay=off toggles, injected as a runtime <style> because the CSS minifier rewrote an authored backdrop-filter override to -webkit- only (would have silently disabled the test in Chrome); shipping stylesheets byte-identical
performance.primary_bottleneck: RESOLVED — CSS backdrop-filter compositing over the live WebGL canvas (primary) plus full-resolution bloom (secondary). Confirmed by the owner's A/B on real hardware, not by this machine's numbers
performance.resolution: round 7 accepted as shipping baseline. Owner verdict on 2020 M1 MacBook Air / Safari: performance DRAMATICALLY SMOOTHER, visual difference TINY and still looks just as good, original lag problem BASICALLY SOLVED
shipping_changes: all four backdrop-filter:blur() layers removed from shipping CSS — zero live backdrop sampling in the built bundle; glass rebuilt from gradient + inset rim + drop shadow at an alpha matched to the blurred original's perceived density
Bloom resolutionScale=0.5 — quarter the fragments, upsampled through the existing mip chain; scene still renders at full DPR 2
performance.do_not_regress: never reintroduce backdrop-filter over the WebGL canvas; do not lower DPR, reduce the 4,892-lead book, simplify or remove the Intelligence Core, or change OrbitControls damping
performance.reference_control: ?legacyfx=1 restores the previous pipeline pixel-for-pixel (mean diff 0, max 0) — preserved
performance.lesson: the bottleneck sat in the compositing stage, which no JavaScript instrument can observe. Frame intervals looked healthy in every round; every subtractive scene toggle returned unchanged because a backdrop blur costs the same regardless of what is behind it; the round-6 matrix on real hardware showed no configuration in distress. What located it was reading the CSS and the owner's subjective A/B
